challenges.narrative: Repository foundations are the point where a project becomes auditable instead of just a folder of files.
challenges.summary: Start from empty or remote projects, then read branch and commit-history signals before changing anything.
challenges.title: Repository Foundations Blueprint Challenge

blocks.body: Every Git command you will ever run moves information between four places. Once you can name them, no command is mysterious - each one is just an arrow between two of these places.

items: Working directory - the files you actually edit.
Staging area - the snapshot you are assembling for the next commit.
Commit history - permanent snapshots, linked into a graph.
HEAD - the marker for where you are standing in that graph.
blocks.title: The places

blocks.caption: add moves edits into staging; commit seals staging into history; HEAD points at where you stand.
blocks.title: Where work flows

blocks.body: A commit is not a 'save' of one file - it is a snapshot of the whole project at one moment, plus a link to the snapshot that came before it. That chain of links is the commit graph you see in the repository diagrams.
Branches and merges are nothing more than names pointing at commits in this graph. When a scenario asks you to 'move a branch' or 'undo a commit', you are really moving pointers and adding snapshots.
blocks.title: Why the graph matters

blocks.body: Editing a file changes only the working directory. Until you stage and commit, Git's history does not know your change exists.
blocks.title: Watch for

blocks.body: Every level starts the same way: look at the repository diagram and status signals first, then decide which arrow you need. The answer is always a repository state, never a memorized command string.

items: Where is the change I care about right now - working directory, staging, or history?
Where does it need to end up?
Which command moves work between exactly those two places?
blocks.title: Before every command, ask

lessons.summary: The four places your work lives - working directory, staging area, commit history, and HEAD - and how every Git command moves changes between them.
lessons.title: How Git Thinks

blocks.body: A Git command starts with `git`, then a verb such as `status`, `add`, or `commit`. Options change behavior; arguments name the thing the command acts on. Angle-bracket words in lessons are placeholders, not text to type literally.
A repository is a working folder plus Git metadata. The working folder is where you edit files. The `.git` directory stores commits, refs, configuration, and the index that powers staging.

lessons.summary: The hidden `.git` directory, tracked files, untracked files, and repository metadata.
lessons.title: What a Repository Is

blocks.body: Git always acts on the repository in your current folder. `cd <folder>` is a shell command - not a Git command - that moves you between folders. It sets the stage: after `git init <name>` or `git clone <url> <folder>` creates a project folder, you `cd` into it before running Git there. In these lessons `cd` is accepted and changes nothing on its own; it simply marks that you have stepped into the project so the Git commands that follow read naturally.

lessons.summary: Using `cd` to step into a repository before you run Git.
lessons.title: Moving Into Your Project

blocks.body: A commit graph is a chain of snapshots. Each commit points to its parent commit. Branches are names pointing at commits, and HEAD tells you which branch or commit you are standing on.

lessons.summary: How commits, parents, branches, and HEAD fit together.
lessons.title: Reading a Commit Graph
